title: The Red-Headed League
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
sourceEdition: The Strand Magazine (1891), Project Gutenberg plain-text edition
sourceJurisdiction: Public domain worldwide (author died 1930; US publication 1891, pre-1929)

premise.en: A red-haired pawnbroker is paid a small fortune to copy an encyclopedia for a mysterious league, and Sherlock Holmes suspects that something far more serious is hidden beneath the strange arrangement.

summary.en: Mr. Jabez Wilson visits Sherlock Holmes with an odd story: a strange organization called the Red-Headed League paid him generously for weeks to copy the encyclopedia, only to dissolve without warning. Holmes, intrigued by the sheer pointlessness of the scheme, suspects it was designed to keep Wilson away from his own shop, and he and Watson set out to discover what has really been happening beneath the pawnbroker's floor.

tutorNotes.pronunciation: Practice the stress pattern in longer words like 'encyclopedia,' 'organization,' and 'pawnbroker,' since misplaced stress can make Holmes's Victorian vocabulary hard to follow aloud. The silent letters in 'Wednesday' and 'business' also trip learners up.
tutorNotes.grammar: This text uses full narrative tenses, including the past perfect for events before the main story ('he had answered the advertisement') and reported speech when characters retell what others said to them. Passive constructions like 'the League was founded' and 'he was told to remain' appear often, since Victorian English favors formal, indirect phrasing.
tutorNotes.culture: Pawnbrokers, who lent money in exchange for holding an item as security, were common on ordinary London streets in the 1890s, and a small business like Wilson's would have relied on a single loyal assistant to survive. Newspaper advertisements were the main way such strange offers reached the public before telephones or radio existed.
tutorNotes.commonErrors: Learners often confuse 'lend' (to give something temporarily, done by the pawnbroker) with 'borrow' (to receive something temporarily, done by the customer). Watch also for 'vacancy' (an open position) versus 'vacant' (empty), both of which appear in the story's newspaper advertisement.

question.en: Why does the Red-Headed League pay Jabez Wilson to copy the encyclopedia?
What clue about Wilson's assistant first makes Holmes suspicious?
What are the criminals actually planning to steal, and how do they plan to reach it?
Why does Holmes wait until Saturday night to act, rather than earlier in the week?
What does the story suggest about why Holmes finds the case interesting despite its strange, almost comic details?

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — A Curious Advertisement
paragraphs: I called upon my friend Sherlock Holmes one autumn day and found him deep in conversation with a stout, red-haired gentleman.
Holmes introduced the visitor as Mr. Jabez Wilson, a pawnbroker of Coburg Square.
His story, Holmes assured me, was the most singular he had listened to for months.
Wilson looked at me with some suspicion at first, but Holmes explained that I had assisted him in many of his most interesting cases before.
Reassured, Wilson pulled a crumpled newspaper from his pocket.
He pointed to an advertisement that he had, he said, answered some eight weeks earlier.
It announced a vacancy in something called the Red-Headed League, open only to men whose hair was a genuine and vivid shade of red.
Wilson explained that his assistant, a sharp young man named Vincent Spaulding, had noticed the advertisement first.
Spaulding had practically insisted that Wilson apply for it without delay.
He had accompanied Wilson to the office, where a small, fierce-looking man examined Wilson's hair with an almost violent enthusiasm.
Wilson was accepted for the position at once, before he had even finished sitting down.
He was told that the League had been founded, according to its odd charter, by an eccentric American millionaire who wished to help red-headed men everywhere.
For four pounds a week, an excellent wage by any measure, Wilson was required only to copy the encyclopedia in the League's office each day.
He could not leave the building during working hours, or he would forfeit his position and his generous income permanently.
This arrangement had continued happily enough for eight weeks, with Wilson copying entries on subjects ranging from Abbots to Archery.
Then, that very morning, everything changed without warning.
When Wilson arrived at the office as usual, he found the door locked.
A small, printed notice had been pinned firmly to it instead.
The notice stated simply that the Red-Headed League had been dissolved as of that date, without any further explanation offered to its confused members.
Wilson had gone at once to the landlord of the building, but the man had never heard of any League.
He knew nothing at all of the tenant who had rented the office and vanished so suddenly.
Bewildered and suddenly without his generous income, Wilson had come straight to Holmes, hoping the detective might explain this strange disappearance.
Holmes asked several further questions about Spaulding, wanting every small detail Wilson could remember about the young man's habits and appearance.
Wilson described him as short, strongly built, and quick in his movements, with a curious white splash of acid on his forehead from some past accident.
He also mentioned, almost as an afterthought, that Spaulding's ears were pierced for earrings, a detail Wilson found unremarkable but which made Holmes sit forward with sudden interest.
I could see that my friend was already forming a picture of this assistant that went far beyond anything Wilson himself suspected.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Holmes Investigates
paragraphs: After Wilson departed, Holmes sat silently for some minutes, his eyes closed and his fingertips pressed together in quiet thought.
He then asked me what I made of Wilson's assistant, Spaulding.
It was a question I had not expected, since Spaulding had seemed a minor detail in the whole affair.
Holmes remarked that Spaulding had suggested the advertisement and had accompanied Wilson to apply for it.
He had clearly benefited from having his employer safely out of the shop each day.
Holmes further noted, with evident satisfaction, that Wilson had mentioned Spaulding's habit of disappearing into the cellar for hours at a time.
Such devotion to an unpaid photography hobby, Holmes suggested, was itself rather suspicious in a young assistant working for such modest wages.
That afternoon, Holmes and I traveled to Wilson's pawnshop in Coburg Square.
Holmes struck the pavement outside sharply with his walking stick several times before knocking on the door.
When a young man answered, Holmes apologized for disturbing him and asked only for directions.
I noticed, though, that he studied the man's knees with unusual, deliberate care while he spoke.
Once we had walked away, Holmes explained his purpose to me.
He had wished to see whether the assistant's trousers were worn and marked at the knees from long hours of kneeling on a hard floor.
They were, and this detail, combined with the man's pale face despite his supposed photography hobby, confirmed a theory Holmes had been forming.
He then led me on a long walk around the neighboring streets, examining the buildings that stood behind Wilson's shop with great and careful interest.
He was particularly interested in a large bank standing on the corner.
It shared its rear wall directly with the pawnshop and the buildings beside it.
Holmes explained that the bank had recently received a large shipment of French gold, thirty thousand coins in all, currently held within its underground vault.
He believed that Spaulding, whose real name was likely quite different from the one he used, was digging a tunnel from Wilson's cellar toward that very vault.
The absurd Red-Headed League, Holmes concluded, had been invented for one purpose alone.
It existed only to remove Wilson from his shop for several hours every single day.
With Wilson safely occupied copying the encyclopedia across town, Spaulding and his accomplices could dig undisturbed beneath the empty building.
The League's sudden end, Holmes reasoned, meant that the tunnel was now finally complete.
I asked how he could be so certain of a bank robbery from such thin and circumstantial evidence, and Holmes admitted that certainty was not yet his, only a strong and reasonable suspicion.
Still, he added, a suspicion built from careful observation was worth pursuing at once, since criminals rarely waited long once their preparations were finished.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — A Night in the Vault
paragraphs: Holmes wired for a police inspector and for the bank's director, a Mr. Merryweather.
He arranged to meet both men that same evening near the bank.
He explained to me that the robbery would surely occur that Saturday night.
Saturday gave the criminals two full days before the bank would reopen and discover the theft.
Merryweather led our small party down into the bank's cellar, where crates of French gold coins were stacked beside the thick stone floor of the vault.
Holmes knelt immediately and examined the stone flooring with his lantern.
He tapped it carefully until he found the place where it sounded hollow beneath his knuckles.
He announced with quiet confidence that the tunnel would soon break through at that exact spot, and he arranged our small party to wait, hidden, in the darkness.
We waited in complete silence and darkness for what felt like hours.
I confess my legs grew stiff and my patience grew thin during the long, tense wait.
At last, a thin line of light appeared between two stones in the floor.
A pale hand emerged, feeling cautiously along the edge of the growing opening.
The hand withdrew suddenly, but a moment later the stone was pushed fully aside.
A young man climbed up into the vault, breathing hard from his effort below.
It was Spaulding, whose true name Holmes later revealed to be John Clay, a clever and dangerous criminal known to the police under several other names.
The instant Clay stood upright, Holmes seized him firmly by the collar, and the inspector's constables closed in swiftly around the tunnel's dark mouth.
A second man attempted to flee back down the tunnel.
He was caught almost immediately by a constable waiting at the entrance on the street above.
Clay, remarkably calm despite his sudden capture, remarked with a strange, cold dignity that the game was now finished.
He said there was nothing more to be done about the matter.
He asked only to be treated with the courtesy owed to a gentleman.
Holmes found this request darkly amusing, given the scale of the crime the man had attempted.
As the prisoners were led away, Merryweather thanked Holmes warmly.
He asked how Holmes had ever managed to trace such an elaborate and carefully hidden scheme.
Holmes only smiled and said that the full explanation would keep until we were both comfortably settled at home, away from the cold and the excitement of the night.
Merryweather pressed a small reward upon him, which Holmes accepted with good humor, remarking that the case itself had already paid him in the coin he valued most.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Explanation
paragraphs: Walking home afterward, Holmes explained his reasoning to me in full.
He clearly enjoyed the chance to lay out each small step of his deduction, one after another.
The Red-Headed League itself, he said, was nothing but an elaborate device.
Its very absurdity was the detail that first caught his attention and would not let it go.
Ordinary criminals do not invent something so strange without a serious purpose behind it.
Four pounds a week, he pointed out, was a small price indeed for access to that particular cellar.
Wilson's own description of Spaulding's worn knees, and his hours spent supposedly developing photographs, told Holmes exactly what kind of work was truly occupying the young man.
From there, it required only a short walk to notice the bank standing directly behind the pawnshop, and the entire scheme became immediately clear to him.
I remarked that Holmes had saved the bank a fortune in French gold.
His skill, I told him, had once again proven far superior to that of the official police.
Holmes smiled and admitted that he had indeed found the case a pleasant distraction from the dull routine of ordinary life in London.
He added that a man in his profession must be grateful for problems that are, at the very least, out of the common way.
Without such curious puzzles, he told me, existence would become a flat and profitless affair.
It would hardly be worth the trouble of living through each gray London day, he added with a faint smile.
It was in the search for these small, strange trifles of daily life, he concluded, that the true, rare pleasures of his profession could still be found.
I told him that his modesty did him credit, but that London was fortunate indeed to have a man of his particular talents watching over its quieter corners.
Holmes laughed at this, waved the compliment aside, and turned the conversation to the ordinary business of the following day, as though the whole strange affair had already ended.
